## The Moon Is Falling {background-image="../../../assets/images/common/eso-milky-way-panoramic.jpg" background-opacity="0.2"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
The Moon IS falling toward Earth.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
Right now. Continuously. Every second.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
But it's moving **sideways** so fast that it keeps **missing**.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .bg-muted .p-2}
That combination of falling + moving sideways is what we call an **orbit**.
:::

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. "Before Newton, 'earthly' physics and 'celestial' physics were separate. Newton unified them with one equation."
:::

{{< fig newtons-cannon >}}

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-muted .text-center}
Fire fast enough → fall *around* Earth instead of hitting it.
:::

::: {.notes}

- Distinguish **mass** (inertia) from **gravitational force** and **apparent weight**

## Where We Left Off (Lecture 5)

Kepler discovered three **empirical laws**:

::: {.incremental}
1. Orbits are **ellipses** with the Sun at one focus
2. Planets sweep **equal areas in equal times**
3. $P^2 \propto a^3$ (period-distance relation)
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
These describe *what* planets do.

But Kepler couldn't explain *why*.
:::

::: {.notes}
4–5 min. "Today, Newton gives us the *why*."
:::

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Part 1: The Rules of Motion
:::

*Newton's Three Laws*

---

## Newton's First Law: Inertia {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl .bg-muted .p-3}
**An object at rest stays at rest. An object in motion stays in motion (constant velocity) — unless acted upon by a net force.**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**Key insight:** Things don't change their motion on their own.

If something speeds up, slows down, or changes direction — a **net force** caused it.
:::

::: {.notes}
5–6 min. "This contradicts Aristotle, who thought motion requires continuous effort."
:::

---

## First Law Example: Deep Space

::: {.quiz}
A spacecraft in deep space fires its engines briefly, then shuts them off. What happens next?

- [ ] It gradually slows down and stops
- [x] It continues at constant velocity indefinitely
- [ ] It starts drifting toward the nearest star
- [ ] It needs to keep firing to maintain speed
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll. "No friction in space = no slowing down."
:::

---

## Newton's Second Law: F = ma {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl .bg-muted .p-3}
$$\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$$

**Net force tells matter how to accelerate.**

**Mass tells matter how much to resist.**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-muted}
Units: force in N, mass in kg, acceleration in m/s².
:::

:::: {.columns .mt-4}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
More net force → more acceleration
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
More mass → less acceleration
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
6–7 min. "The arrow notation means these are vectors — direction matters."
:::

---

## Quick Check: F = ma {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
The same force is applied to a bowling ball and a tennis ball. Which experiences greater acceleration?

- [ ] The bowling ball (more mass)
- [x] The tennis ball (less mass)
- [ ] Both experience the same acceleration
- [ ] Neither accelerates
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

---

## Critical Insight: Direction Changes = Acceleration {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
**Constant speed ≠ constant velocity**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
Acceleration happens when *either* changes:

- Speeding up ✓
- Slowing down ✓
- **Changing direction at constant speed** ✓
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .bg-warning-subtle .p-2}
A planet moving in a circle at constant speed **is accelerating** because its direction constantly changes!
:::

::: {.notes}
7–8 min. "This is the key to understanding orbits. Circular motion requires a force."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Circular Motion {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
A car drives around a circular track at a constant speedometer reading of 60 mph. Is the car accelerating?

- [ ] No — the speed is constant
- [x] Yes — the direction is constantly changing
- [ ] Only if the driver presses the gas pedal
- [ ] Only if there's friction
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll. "The tires push sideways — that's the centripetal force."
:::

---

## Centripetal Acceleration {background-color="black"}

For circular motion at speed $v$ and radius $r$:

$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$$

::: {.fragment}
This acceleration points **toward the center**.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**The force required:**

$$F_c = ma_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$
:::

::: {.notes}
8–9 min. "Centripetal means 'center-seeking.' Something has to provide this force."
:::

---

## What Provides the Centripetal Force?

**Centripetal force is not a new type of force.**

It's whatever force happens to be pulling the object toward the center:

::: {.incremental}
- For **planets**: gravity
- For a ball on a **string**: tension
- For a **car turning**: friction between tires and road
:::

::: {.notes}
9–10 min. "For orbits, gravity provides the centripetal force."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Centripetal Force {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
A planet orbits the Sun in a nearly circular orbit. What force provides the centripetal acceleration?

- [ ] The planet's inertia
- [ ] The planet's momentum
- [x] Gravity from the Sun
- [ ] The planet's rotational spin
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

---

## Newton's Third Law: Action-Reaction {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl .bg-muted .p-3}
**For every force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force.**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
Examples:

- You push on the ground → the ground pushes back on you
- Earth pulls on the Moon → the Moon pulls on Earth
- Sun pulls on Jupiter → Jupiter pulls on the Sun
:::

::: {.notes}
10–11 min. "The forces are equal. The accelerations are not — because masses differ."
:::

---

## The Astronomical Payoff {background-color="black"}

::: {.text-center}
Jupiter pulls on the Sun with the **same force** the Sun pulls on Jupiter.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
But the Sun is 1000× more massive, so it accelerates 1000× less.

The Sun **wobbles** — just barely.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .bg-success-subtle .p-2}
This tiny stellar wobble is **one major way** we detect exoplanets!
:::

::: {.notes}
11–12 min. "The radial velocity method — we see the star wobble and infer the planet."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Third Law {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
Earth exerts a gravitational force on the Moon. The Moon exerts a force on Earth that is:

- [ ] Much weaker, because the Moon is smaller
- [ ] Much stronger, because Earth is closer
- [x] Exactly equal in magnitude, opposite in direction
- [ ] Zero, because the Moon is in space
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll. "Forces equal, accelerations differ."
:::

Part 2: Universal Gravitation
:::

*One equation rules all*

---

## Predict First! {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
If you **double** your distance from Earth's center, gravity becomes...
:::

:::: {.columns .mt-4}
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment}
A) 1/2 as strong
:::
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment}
B) 1/4 as strong ✓
:::
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment}
C) 1/8 as strong
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
30 sec. Have students vote before revealing.
:::

## Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl .bg-muted .p-3}
$$F_g = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
| Part | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| $G$ | Universal constant ($6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg²) |
| $m_1 m_2$ | Force depends on *both* masses |
| $r^2$ | Force weakens with distance **squared** |
:::

::: {.notes}
12–14 min. "The same equation works for apples, moons, and galaxies."
Assumptions (briefly): works well when objects act like point masses / spherically symmetric bodies, and in the Newtonian regime.
:::

---

## {background-color="black"}

{{< fig gravity-equation-visual >}}

::: {.notes}
14–15 min. Let the visual speak.
:::

---

## The Inverse-Square Law {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
"$r^2$ in the denominator" is profound:
:::

| Distance change | Force change |
|-----------------|--------------|
| Double the distance | Force drops to **1/4** |
| Triple the distance | Force drops to **1/9** |
| 10× the distance | Force drops to **1/100** |

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Physical intuition:** Gravitational influence spreads over sphere surfaces.

Sphere area grows like $r^2$ → effect per area drops like $1/r^2$.
:::

::: {.notes}
15–16 min. "Like light spreading from a flashlight — same total, more area, less per spot."
:::

---

## {background-color="black"}

{{< fig inverse-square-diagram >}}

::: {.notes}
16–17 min. Visual explanation of inverse-square spreading.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Inverse-Square {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
The Moon is about 60 Earth radii from Earth's center. The Moon experiences gravitational acceleration that is:

- [ ] 60 times weaker
- [ ] 360 times weaker
- [x] 3,600 times weaker
- [ ] The same strength
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-sm}
**Solution:** At 60× the distance: $1/60^2 = 1/3600$.
:::

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. iClicker poll, then explain.
:::

---

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Mass vs. Weight
:::

*A critical distinction*

---

## The Distinction {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

| Quantity | What it measures | Changes with location? |
|----------|------------------|------------------------|
| **Mass** ($m$) | Resistance to acceleration (inertia) | **No** — same everywhere |
| **Gravitational force** ($F_g$) | Force from gravity | **Yes** — depends on local $g$ |
| **Apparent weight** | What you *feel* (scale reading) | **Yes** — depends on gravity AND motion |

::: {.notes}
17–18 min. "Mass is intrinsic. Weight depends on where you are."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Mass vs. Weight {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
An astronaut has mass 70 kg on Earth. On the Moon (gravity ~1/6 as strong), their:

- [ ] Mass decreases to about 12 kg
- [x] Scale reading decreases to ~1/6, but mass stays 70 kg
- [ ] Both mass and scale reading stay the same
- [ ] Mass increases because there's less gravity
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

---

## {.center background-color="black"}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Why Astronauts Float
:::

*Fixing the biggest misconception*

---

## The Wrong Answer {background-color="#dc2626"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
❌ "Astronauts float because there's no gravity in space."
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
At ISS altitude (~400 km), Earth's gravity is still **~90%** as strong as at the surface!
:::

::: {.notes}
18–19 min. "This is one of the most common misconceptions in physics."
:::

---

## The Right Answer {background-color="#16a34a"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
✓ Astronauts float because they're in **free fall**.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
The ISS and everyone inside are falling toward Earth together.

But moving sideways so fast they keep missing.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
Everything falls together at the same rate → nothing pushes back on you → **no sensation of weight**.
:::

::: {.notes}
19–20 min. "You haven't escaped gravity. You've eliminated the floor's push."
:::

---

## {background-color="black"}

{{< fig free-fall-astronaut >}}

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-muted .text-center}
**Free fall = apparent weightlessness**

Not because gravity is gone — because everything is falling together.
:::

::: {.notes}
20–21 min. Let the image drive it home.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Weightlessness {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
An astronaut floats inside the ISS, 400 km above Earth. Earth's gravitational pull on the astronaut is:

- [ ] Zero — that's why they float
- [x] About 90% of what it would be on Earth's surface
- [ ] Exactly the same as on Earth's surface
- [ ] Much stronger than on Earth's surface
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

## {.center background-color="black"}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Part 3: Newton Explains Kepler
:::

*From patterns to physics*

---

## The Big Picture

| Kepler's Law | Newton's Explanation |
|--------------|---------------------|
| Orbits are **ellipses** | Inverse-square force → conic sections |
| **Equal areas** in equal times | Central force → angular momentum conserved |
| $P^2 \propto a^3$ | Inverse-square gives this exact exponent |

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center}
**Kepler said "here's what happens."**

**Newton said "here's why it must happen."**
:::

::: {.notes}
21–23 min. "All three laws flow from one equation."
:::

---

## Explaining Kepler I: Ellipses {background-color="black"}

**Question:** Why are orbits ellipses?

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**Newton's Answer:**

Any object moving under an **inverse-square central force** traces a **conic section**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Not enough energy to escape → **ellipse**
- Just enough energy to escape → **parabola**
- More than escape energy → **hyperbola**
:::

::: {.notes}
23–24 min. "The shape is a CONSEQUENCE of inverse-square, not an assumption."
:::

---

## {background-color="black"}

{{< fig conic-sections-orbits >}}

::: {.notes}
24–25 min. Visual of conic sections.
:::

---

## Quick Check: First Law Explained {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
Newton explained that planetary orbits are ellipses because:

- [ ] Planets were created in elliptical paths
- [x] Inverse-square gravity mathematically produces conic sections
- [ ] Ellipses are the simplest possible curves
- [ ] The Sun's rotation shapes the orbits
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

---

## Explaining Kepler II: Equal Areas {background-color="black"}

**Question:** Why do planets sweep equal areas in equal times?

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**Newton's Answer:**

Gravity is a **central force** — always pointing toward the Sun.

Central forces **conserve angular momentum**.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
If $L$ is constant and you get closer ($r$ smaller), you must move faster ($v$ larger).
:::

::: {.notes}
25–26 min. "Same physics as the ice skater pulling arms in."
:::

---

## The Ice Skater (Again) {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Arms in** → spins **faster**

(smaller $r$)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Arms out** → spins **slower**

(larger $r$)
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center}
**Conservation of angular momentum.**

Same physics for planets: closer → faster, farther → slower.
:::

::: {.notes}
26–27 min. "Kepler described the pattern. Newton explained the mechanism."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Second Law Explained {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
Newton explained Kepler's Second Law (equal areas) as a consequence of:

- [ ] The inverse-square nature of gravity
- [x] Conservation of angular momentum because gravity is a central force
- [ ] The fact that planets have elliptical orbits
- [ ] Energy conservation
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

---

## Explaining Kepler III: $P^2 \propto a^3$ {background-color="black"}

**Question:** Why this exact relationship?

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**Newton's Answer:**

For a force $F \propto 1/r^n$, the period-distance relationship is:

$$P^2 \propto a^{n+1}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
- If $n = 2$ (inverse-square): $P^2 \propto a^3$ ✓
- If $n = 1$: $P^2 \propto a^2$ ✗
- If $n = 3$: $P^2 \propto a^4$ ✗
:::

::: {.notes}
27–28 min. "Only inverse-square matches Kepler's observations!"
:::

---

## Newton's Improved Version {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .bg-muted .p-3}
$$P^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{G(M + m)} a^3$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**What's new compared to Kepler:**

- The constant includes $G$ and the **total mass**
- Works for **any** gravitational system, not just our Solar System
- **We can solve for mass!**
:::

::: {.notes}
28–29 min. "This is the mass-measuring power tool."
:::

---

## Motion Reveals Mass {background-color="black"}

Rearranging Newton's version:

$$M \approx \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{G P^2}$$

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center .text-xl}
**Measure orbital period and distance → Calculate central mass**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-muted}
This is how we "weigh" the Sun, black holes, and galaxies.

We never touch them — we just watch how things move around them.
:::

::: {.notes}
29–31 min. "This technique will come up again and again."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Weighing the Sun {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
How do astronomers determine the mass of the Sun?

- [ ] By measuring how bright it is
- [x] By measuring Earth's orbital period and distance
- [ ] By sending a spacecraft to collect a sample
- [ ] By measuring the Sun's size
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Different Stars {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
Two planets orbit different stars at the same distance. Planet A orbits a 2 $M_\odot$ star. Planet B orbits a 0.5 $M_\odot$ star. Which has the shorter orbital period?

- [x] Planet A (around the more massive star)
- [ ] Planet B (around the less massive star)
- [ ] Both have the same period
- [ ] Cannot determine without knowing planet masses
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-sm}
**More massive star → stronger gravity → faster orbits → shorter period.**
:::

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. iClicker poll, then explain.
:::

---

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Part 4: Synthesis
:::

*From empirical to physical*

---

## From Kepler to Newton {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

| Kepler (Empirical) | Newton (Physical) |
|-------------------|-------------------|
| Describes *what* planets do | Explains *why* they do it |
| Patterns from data | Mechanisms from principles |
| Limited to observed systems | Universal — applies everywhere |
| Can predict within Solar System | Can predict **anywhere gravity acts** |

::: {.notes}
31–33 min. "This is the transition from pattern to physics."
:::

---

## One Equation Rules All {background-color="black"}

::: {.text-center}
$$F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
With this single equation, Newton explained:

- Why apples fall
- Why the Moon orbits Earth
- Why planets orbit the Sun
- Why all three of Kepler's laws hold
- How to weigh objects we'll never touch
:::

::: {.notes}
33–34 min. "One of the greatest unifications in the history of science."
:::

---

## Key Takeaways {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-sm}

1. **Newton's Three Laws:** (1) Inertia, (2) $F = ma$, (3) Action-Reaction

2. **Circular motion = acceleration** (direction changes), requiring centripetal force

3. **Universal Gravitation:** $F = GMm/r^2$ — inverse-square law

4. **Mass vs. Weight:** Mass is intrinsic; weight depends on local gravity

5. **Astronauts float because of free fall** — not because gravity is absent!

6. **Newton explains Kepler:**
   - Ellipses → inverse-square force
   - Equal areas → angular momentum conservation
   - $P^2 \propto a^3$ → inverse-square gives this exponent

7. **Motion reveals mass:** $M = 4\pi^2 a^3/(GP^2)$

:::

::: {.notes}
34–36 min. Rapid recap.
:::

---

## The Course Connection {background-color="black"}

::: {.text-center}
**Motion reveals mass** — the foundation for nearly everything else:
:::

::: {.incremental .mt-4}
- **Stars:** Binary star orbits → stellar masses
- **Galaxies:** Rotation curves → dark matter
- **Black holes:** Orbiting stars → invisible mass
- **Exoplanets:** Stellar wobbles → planet detection
:::

::: {.notes}
36–38 min. "We'll use Newton's insight over and over."

## {.center background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Numerical Verification
:::

*Newton's claim: the Moon is falling*

::: {.notes}
Let's verify Newton's revolutionary claim with actual numbers.
:::

---

## The Moon IS Falling: Calculation {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Newton's claim:** The same gravity that pulls apples pulls the Moon.

**Test:** Calculate the Moon's centripetal acceleration and compare to surface gravity.

::: {.fragment}
**Given data:**

- Earth-Moon distance: $r = 384,400$ km $= 3.844 \times 10^8$ m
- Moon's orbital period: $P = 27.3$ days
- Earth's radius: $R_E = 6,371$ km
- Surface gravity: $g = 9.81$ m/s²
:::

::: {.notes}
"Let's verify Newton's claim quantitatively. This is the calculation that unified heaven and Earth."
:::

---

## Step 1: Find the Moon's Orbital Speed {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

The Moon travels a circular path of circumference $2\pi r$ in time $P$.

::: {.fragment}
**Convert period to seconds:**

$$P = 27.3 \text{ days} \times \frac{24 \text{ hr}}{1 \text{ day}} \times \frac{3600 \text{ s}}{1 \text{ hr}} = 2.36 \times 10^6 \text{ s}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Calculate orbital speed:**

$$v = \frac{2\pi r}{P} = \frac{2\pi \times 3.844 \times 10^8 \text{ m}}{2.36 \times 10^6 \text{ s}}$$

$$v = \frac{2.415 \times 10^9 \text{ m}}{2.36 \times 10^6 \text{ s}} = 1,023 \text{ m/s} \approx 1.0 \text{ km/s}$$
:::

::: {.notes}
"The Moon moves at about 1 km/s. Not that fast by space standards, but remember it's very far away."
:::

---

## Step 2: Calculate Centripetal Acceleration {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{(1,023 \text{ m/s})^2}{3.844 \times 10^8 \text{ m}}$$

::: {.fragment}
$$a_c = \frac{1.047 \times 10^6 \text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2}{3.844 \times 10^8 \text{ m}} = 2.72 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m/s}^2$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**Unit check:** $\frac{\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2}{\text{m}} = \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}$ ✓ (acceleration)
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
The Moon's acceleration toward Earth is $a_c = 0.00272$ m/s².

**Compare to surface gravity:** $g = 9.81$ m/s².
:::

::: {.notes}
"Always check your units. If they don't work out to m/s² for acceleration, you made a mistake."
:::

---

## Step 3: Test the Inverse-Square Law {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**If gravity follows** $1/r^2$, then at the Moon's distance:

$$\frac{a_{\text{Moon}}}{g_{\text{surface}}} = \frac{1}{(\text{distance ratio})^2}$$

::: {.fragment}
**Calculate distance ratio:**

$$\frac{r_{\text{Moon}}}{R_E} = \frac{3.844 \times 10^8 \text{ m}}{6.371 \times 10^6 \text{ m}} = 60.3$$

The Moon is **60.3 Earth radii** away.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Predicted acceleration ratio:**

$$\frac{a_{\text{Moon}}}{g} = \frac{1}{(60.3)^2} = \frac{1}{3636} = 2.75 \times 10^{-4}$$
:::

::: {.notes}
"Now we compare prediction to measurement."
:::

---

## Step 4: Compare Prediction to Measurement {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Predicted** (from inverse-square):

$$a_{\text{predicted}} = \frac{g}{3636} = \frac{9.81}{3636} = 2.70 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m/s}^2$$

**Measured** (from orbital motion):

$$a_{\text{measured}} = 2.72 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m/s}^2$$

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .bg-success-subtle .p-2 .text-center}
**Match!** Difference < 1%

**The same gravity that pulls apples pulls the Moon.**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-muted}
This was Newton's triumph: unifying terrestrial and celestial physics.
:::

::: {.notes}
"Newton showed that there's no separate 'celestial physics.' The same laws work everywhere."
:::

---

## Verifying ISS "Weightlessness" {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Claim:** At ISS altitude (400 km), gravity is still ~90% of surface value.

::: {.fragment}
**Calculate:**

$$r_{\text{ISS}} = R_E + h = 6,371 + 400 = 6,771 \text{ km}$$

$$\frac{g_{\text{ISS}}}{g_{\text{surface}}} = \left(\frac{R_E}{r_{\text{ISS}}}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{6,371}{6,771}\right)^2$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$= (0.941)^2 = 0.885 = 88.5\%$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .bg-warning-subtle .p-2}
**Gravity at ISS altitude is 88.5% of surface gravity!**

Astronauts float because they're **falling**, not because gravity is gone.
:::

::: {.notes}
"400 km sounds high, but it's only 6% farther from Earth's center. Gravity barely decreases."
:::

---

## Weighing the Sun: Full Calculation {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Given:**

- Earth's orbital period: $P = 365.25$ days $= 3.156 \times 10^7$ s
- Earth's orbital radius: $a = 1.496 \times 10^{11}$ m (1 AU)
- $G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg²

::: {.fragment}
**From Newton's form of Kepler III:**

$$M_\odot = \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{G P^2}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$M_\odot = \frac{4\pi^2 (1.496 \times 10^{11})^3}{(6.674 \times 10^{-11})(3.156 \times 10^7)^2}$$
:::

::: {.notes}
"Let's compute this step by step with careful unit tracking."
:::

---

## Weighing the Sun: Unit Analysis {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.text-sm}
$$M_\odot = \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{G P^2}$$

**Numerator units:**

$$[\text{m}^3] \quad \text{(since } a^3 \text{ is in meters cubed)}$$

**Denominator units:**

$$\left[\frac{\text{N} \cdot \text{m}^2}{\text{kg}^2}\right] \times [\text{s}^2] = \left[\frac{\text{kg} \cdot \text{m/s}^2 \cdot \text{m}^2}{\text{kg}^2}\right] \times [\text{s}^2] = \frac{\text{m}^3}{\text{kg}}$$

::: {.fragment}
**Result units:**

$$\frac{\text{m}^3}{\text{m}^3/\text{kg}} = \text{kg} \quad \checkmark$$
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
"The units work out to kg, which is what we want for mass. Always check!"
:::

---

## Weighing the Sun: Result {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Calculating numerator:**

$$4\pi^2 (1.496 \times 10^{11})^3 = 4\pi^2 \times 3.348 \times 10^{33} = 1.322 \times 10^{35} \text{ m}^3$$

**Calculating denominator:**

$$(6.674 \times 10^{-11})(3.156 \times 10^7)^2 = 6.674 \times 10^{-11} \times 9.96 \times 10^{14}$$
$$= 6.65 \times 10^{4} \text{ m}^3/\text{kg}$$

::: {.fragment}
**Final result:**

$$M_\odot = \frac{1.322 \times 10^{35}}{6.65 \times 10^{4}} = 1.99 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .bg-success-subtle .p-2}
**The Sun's mass is $2 \times 10^{30}$ kg** — determined just by watching Earth orbit!
:::

::: {.notes}
"We weighed an object 150 million km away, using only geometry and timing."
:::

---

## {.center background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Deeper Dive
:::

*Escape velocity and orbital energy*

::: {.notes}
Optional advanced content.
:::

---

## Escape Velocity {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

**Question:** How fast must you launch an object so it never falls back?

::: {.fragment}
**Energy conservation:**

$$\frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{GMm}{r} = 0$$

(Kinetic energy at launch = gravitational potential energy to escape)
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Solving for escape velocity:**

$$v_{\text{escape}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}$$
:::

::: {.notes}
"This is the minimum speed to escape a gravitational well."
:::

---

## Earth's Escape Velocity: Calculation {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

$$v_{\text{escape}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM_E}{R_E}}$$

**Given:**

- $G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg²
- $M_E = 5.97 \times 10^{24}$ kg
- $R_E = 6.371 \times 10^6$ m

::: {.fragment}
$$v_{\text{escape}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 6.674 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.97 \times 10^{24}}{6.371 \times 10^6}}$$

$$= \sqrt{\frac{7.97 \times 10^{14}}{6.371 \times 10^6}} = \sqrt{1.25 \times 10^8} \text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$v_{\text{escape}} = 11,200 \text{ m/s} = \boxed{11.2 \text{ km/s}}$$
:::

::: {.notes}
"To escape Earth, you need 11.2 km/s — about 40,000 km/hr or Mach 33."
:::

---

## Escape Velocities Across the Solar System {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

| Object | Mass (Earth = 1) | Radius (Earth = 1) | $v_{\text{escape}}$ |
|--------|------------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Moon | 0.012 | 0.27 | 2.4 km/s |
| Earth | 1 | 1 | 11.2 km/s |
| Jupiter | 318 | 11.2 | 59.5 km/s |
| Sun | 333,000 | 109 | 618 km/s |

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Notice:** $v_{\text{escape}} \propto \sqrt{M/R}$

Jupiter is massive but also large → moderate increase in escape velocity.
:::

::: {.notes}
"Escape velocity depends on the ratio M/R, not mass alone."
:::

---

## Circular Orbital Velocity {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

For a **circular orbit**, set gravitational force = centripetal force:

$$\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$

::: {.fragment}
**Solving for orbital velocity:**

$$v_{\text{circular}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .bg-muted .p-2}
**Key relationship:**

$$v_{\text{escape}} = \sqrt{2} \times v_{\text{circular}}$$

To escape, you need only **41% more speed** than circular orbit speed!
:::

::: {.notes}
"This is why it's relatively easy to send probes to other planets once you're in orbit."
:::
